question: What is the fundamental concept of the GMDSS?
choices: GMDSS utilizes automated systems and satellite technology to improve emergency communications for the world’s shipping industry.
It is intended to automate and improve existing digital selective calling procedures and techniques.
It is intended to provide more effective but lower cost commercial communications.
It is intended to provide compulsory vessels with a collision avoidance system when they are operating in waters that are also occupied by non-compulsory vessels.
explanation: GMDSS replaced the old manual Morse and voice watch system with automated distress alerting (DSC, EPIRBs) and satellite communications, so distress alerts reach rescue authorities reliably anywhere at sea.
background: GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) became mandatory in 1999 under SOLAS Chapter IV (SOLAS = the IMO Safety Of Life At Sea convention). Before it, ships kept a manual Morse (500 kHz) and voice watch and relied on ships nearby hearing them. Now an alert goes automatically to an RCC (Rescue Coordination Centre) ashore, which then coordinates SAR (search and rescue) with nearby ships.

question: The primary purpose of the GMDSS is:
choices: Allow more effective control of SAR situations by vessels.
Automate and improve emergency communications for the world's shipping industry.
Provide additional shipboard systems for more effective company communications.
Effective and inexpensive communications.
explanation: The purpose of GMDSS is to automate and improve distress and safety communications for shipping. Commercial communications are a side benefit, not the goal.

background: Sea areas are defined by which shore stations can hear a ship's DSC alert. A1: a VHF coast station with continuous Ch-70 watch (~20-30 NM). question: What statement best describes modulation?
choices: Imposing intelligence onto a radio carrier signal.
Changing mark-space to 1 and 0.
Adjusting the frequency to the optimum band for long distance communications.
Converting the carrier from a low frequency to a higher frequency.
explanation: Modulation is impressing information (voice, data) onto a radio-frequency carrier by varying its amplitude, frequency or phase.
background: Modulation puts information onto a carrier. AM varies the amplitude, FM varies the frequency, and PM varies the phase (marine VHF is really PM, designated G3E/F3E). SSB (single sideband) transmits only one sideband of an AM signal, without the carrier. That halves the bandwidth and puts all the power into useful signal, which is why MF/HF marine voice uses SSB.

question: What sequence best describes an MF-HF DSC Distress Alert transmission?

explanation: An MF/HF DSC distress alert: dot pattern (to stop scanning receivers), format/distress code, own MMSI, nature of distress, position and time, follow-on communications type (emission), then end. The pool's listed sequence is the closest.
background: A DSC message is a short digital packet: dot pattern (wakes up scanning receivers), format specifier (distress / all ships / individual / group / area), address, category (distress, urgency, safety, routine), sender's MMSI, nature of distress, position and time, follow-on mode (J3E voice or F1B telex), end of sequence (EOS) and error check character (ECC). Each character is 10 bits and the whole message is sent twice.

question: Your ship received a Distress relay from a coast station on DSC frequency 2187.5 kHz. What action should the watch officer take?
choices: Retransmit the DSC call on 2187.5 kHz to other vessels in the vicinity to assist in SAR operations.
Monitor 2182.0 kHz to determine if there are any genuine Distress communications.
Transmit a voice “Mayday Relay” call on 2187.5 kHz to other vessels in the vicinity.
Transmit a voice “Mayday Relay” call on 2182.0 kHz to other vessels in the vicinity.
explanation: After a coast station's DSC relay on 2187.5 kHz, monitor 2182.0 kHz for the actual distress traffic. Don't relay further yourself.
background: A 'distress relay' is an alert re-sent on behalf of another station, normally by a coast station or RCC to ships in the area. Ships should not add their own DSC relays, because duplicate alerts flood the system. Relay (preferably to a coast station or RCC, by voice) only if the original wasn't acknowledged and no one else is handling it, and only on the Master's decision.

question: What action should you take after sending a false or mistaken Distress alert on VHF?
choices: Make a voice announcement to cancel the alert on Ch-16.
Send a DSC cancellation message on Ch-70.
Make a voice announcement to cancel the alert on Ch-13.
Make a voice announcement to cancel the alert on Ch-22A.
explanation: Cancel a false VHF DSC alert with a voice announcement on Ch-16 ('All stations x3, this is…, cancel my distress alert of…'). Many radios also send a DSC cancel.
choice_notes: There is no DSC 'cancel' for VHF in the rules. Cancel by voice.
background: False alert procedure: switch off/reset the equipment immediately, then cancel by voice to 'ALL STATIONS' on the paired voice frequency in each band used (Ch-16, 2182 kHz, 8291 kHz...): 'ALL STATIONS x3, this is (name, call sign, MMSI), position, cancel my distress alert of (date, time UTC).' A false Inmarsat alert is cancelled with a distress-priority message to the RCC via the same LES.

question: What is the fundamental purpose for imposing radio silence?
choices: To ensure that interference to proprietary communications is minimized.
To ensure that only voice communications can be effected on the Distress frequency or channel.
To ensure that a Distressed vessel will have a "window" twice each hour for transmitting routine messages.
To mitigate the risk of interference on a frequency or channel being used for emergency communications.
explanation: Radio silence keeps a distress frequency clear of interference while emergency communications are under way.
background: Radio silence terms: SEELONCE MAYDAY = imposed by the station controlling distress traffic; all others stop transmitting there. SEELONCE DISTRESS = imposed by another station near the casualty. PRUDONCE = restricted working may resume. SEELONCE FEENEE = distress traffic finished, normal use resumes. On NBDP: SILENCE MAYDAY / SILENCE FINI.

question: When can routine communications be resumed after radio silence has been imposed?
choices: Routine communications can resume after the Rescue Coordination Center transmits a message on the frequency or channel being used for emergency communications stating that such traffic has concluded.
After determining that the frequency or channel appears to be no longer in use.
After determining that geographic distance from the Distress situation will prohibit any other signal from interfering with emergency communications.
If, in the master's opinion, communications on that frequency will interfere with emergency communications.
explanation: Normal traffic may resume only after the RCC (or controlling station) announces on that frequency that distress traffic has ended ('SEELONCE FEENEE').
background: Radio silence terms: SEELONCE MAYDAY = imposed by the station controlling distress traffic; all others stop transmitting there. SEELONCE DISTRESS = imposed by another station near the casualty. PRUDONCE = restricted working may resume. SEELONCE FEENEE = distress traffic finished, normal use resumes. On NBDP: SILENCE MAYDAY / SILENCE FINI.

question: What is meant by the term "Seelonce Mayday”?
choices: Stations remaining off the air to safeguard proprietary information.
Stations not directly involved with the on-going Distress communications may not transmit on the Distress frequency or channel.
Two three-minute silent periods, at 15 and 45 minutes after the hour that provide a transmitting "window" for distressed vessels to transmit Distress alerts using J3E.
Communications on a Distress frequency or channel is banned for 24 hours following the cessation of the Distress traffic.
explanation: 'SEELONCE MAYDAY' orders all stations not involved in the distress to stop transmitting on that frequency.

choices: By the Land Earth Station (LES) controlling the Distress communications on that frequency.
By the nearest Public Correspondence Coast Station.
By the On-scene Coordinator (OSC) or the RCC chosen by the SAR Mission Coordinator.
By the vessel first responding to the Distress call.

question: How are normal working conditions restored on a SITOR (NBDP) frequency on which radio silence had been imposed?

The High Seas Service (HSS) that imposed the radio silence must transmit a narrow band direct printing message on the Distress frequency stating "SILENCE FINI".
explanation: On an NBDP frequency, the RCC or coast station that imposed silence lifts it by transmitting 'SILENCE FINI' in SITOR.

question: How are normal working conditions restored after radio silence has been imposed?
choices: All of these answers are correct.
The Land Earth Station (LES) that imposed the radio silence must transmit a voice message on the Distress frequency stating "SILENCE FINI".

question: The Radiotelephone Urgency signal is:
choices: Mayday
Securite
Pan Pan
Seelonce Feenee
explanation: The urgency signal is 'PAN PAN', spoken three times.
background: The four priorities, from highest: DISTRESS (MAYDAY), grave and imminent danger requiring immediate help; URGENCY (PAN PAN), safety of a ship or person is threatened but not imminently (man overboard, engine failure near rocks, medical: PAN PAN MEDICO); SAFETY (SECURITE), important navigational or weather warnings; ROUTINE, everything else.

question: Which of the following situations would normally use the Urgency priority?
choices: A crewmember falling over the side.
A serious medical situation involving a crewmember with potential loss of life.
An important meteorological warning concerning hazardous weather.
A cargo shift or weather situation considered to be of greater hazard than would justify a Safety priority designation.
explanation: Urgency priority suits a situation serious enough to threaten ship or crew but not grave and imminent danger, e.g. a dangerous cargo shift or weather beyond a mere safety message.
background: The four priorities, from highest: DISTRESS (MAYDAY), grave and imminent danger requiring immediate help; URGENCY (PAN PAN), safety of a ship or person is threatened but not imminently (man overboard, engine failure near rocks, medical: PAN PAN MEDICO); SAFETY (SECURITE), important navigational or weather warnings; ROUTINE, everything else.

question: Which of the following situations would NOT properly use the Urgency priority?
choices: Abandoning the vessel just before sinking.
Treatment of a crewmember breaking a leg in a cargo hold.
Leaking oil from a minor tank fracture requiring a mandatory pollution report.
An unexpected deviation in the forecast track line of a typhoon.
explanation: Abandoning a sinking ship is grave and imminent danger, which is DISTRESS (MAYDAY), not urgency.
background: The four priorities, from highest: DISTRESS (MAYDAY), grave and imminent danger requiring immediate help; URGENCY (PAN PAN), safety of a ship or person is threatened but not imminently (man overboard, engine failure near rocks, medical: PAN PAN MEDICO); SAFETY (SECURITE), important navigational or weather warnings; ROUTINE, everything else.

choices: A collision with the ship taking on water.
A serious medical situation involving a crewmember.

explanation: A serious medical case aboard (needing medical advice or evacuation) uses urgency priority (PAN PAN, often PAN PAN MEDICO).

choices: Messages concerning the Safety of Life At Sea (SOLAS).

question: If the Watch Officer hears "PAN PAN" spoken 3 times it means:
choices: A navigation or important meteorological warning should follow.
The station is preparing to transmit a Safety message possibly concerning the safety of a mobile unit or person.
None of these answers is correct.
A mobile unit is in need of immediate assistance.
explanation: PAN PAN x3 introduces an urgency message about the safety of a ship or person. It isn't a navigational/weather warning (that's SECURITE), and not immediate assistance (that's MAYDAY). None of the listed answers is correct.

question: When the GMDSS Radio Operator on watch hears "Securite" spoken three times, he can expect to receive the following information:
choices: The safety of vessel or person is in jeopardy.
A message concerning the Safety of navigation.
A vessel is in need of immediate assistance.
A Coast Station sending an important traffic list.
explanation: SECURITE x3 introduces a safety message: an important navigational or meteorological warning.
background: SECURITE ('say-cure-ee-tay', from French sécurité) announces a safety message: a navigational hazard (drifting containers, unlit buoy, wreck), a gale or storm warning, or other important meteorological information. A safety call is usually announced on Ch-16 or 2182 kHz (or by DSC) and the message itself is given on a working channel.

question: Which of the following steps should be taken, if possible, when the vessel must be abandoned because of a Distress situation?

background: COSPAS-SARSAT (Russian/US/French/Canadian, now international) detects 406 MHz beacons. question: For RF communications, "modulation" is best defined as:
choices: Using a single carrier frequency with the proper power level.

Setting up the transceiver with the correct bandwidth to ensure proper communications.
The combination of the received frequency and oscillator frequency in the mixer.

question: Which of the following keystrokes or characters is sent as part of ARQ communications to request a direct TELEX call to a shore-based location?

question: Which of the following statements concerning SITOR (NBDP) communications is true?
choices: Communication is established on the working channel and answerbacks are exchanged before FEC broadcasts can be received.
All of these answers are true.
Weather broadcasts cannot be made in FEC because sending each character twice would cause the broadcast to be prohibitively long.
Two-way communication with the coast radio station using FEC is not necessary to be able to receive the broadcasts.
explanation: FEC broadcasts are one-way. A ship can receive them without ever contacting the coast station.
background: FEC (collective, BFEC) = one-way to all stations, used for broadcasts (MSI, NAVTEX, distress telex follow-on to all). Each character is sent twice, 280 ms apart (time diversity), so static crashes are less likely to wipe out both copies. SFEC = one-way to one selected station (using its SELCAL), which can receive while staying silent, e.g. under radio silence.

question: Which of the following is true of SITOR (NBDP) in FEC mode, in the presence of static crashes.
choices: FEC reduces the error rate by transmitting each character twice.
Data flow rate depends on signal propagation.
Idle characters are sent upon request.
Transmitter and receiver do not synchronize.
explanation: FEC sends each character twice, so a character hit by a static crash can usually be recovered from its other copy.

question: If the vessel is within range of NAVTEX broadcasts and both the Inmarsat-C and the NAVTEX receiver are inoperative the GMDSS operator should:

background: MSI backup paths: if the NAVTEX receiver fails, tune the MF/HF console to 518 kHz in FEC mode; if outside NAVTEX range, receive HF MSI on the HF NBDP MSI frequencies in FEC; if Inmarsat-C fails, use NAVTEX or HF MSI. question: The "short rules" of propagation necessary to select the appropriate frequency band are:
choices: Shorter distance = Higher Frequency, Daytime = Higher Frequency.
Shorter distance = Lower Frequency, Daytime = Higher Frequency.
Shorter distance = Higher Frequency, Daytime = Lower Frequency.
Shorter distance = Lower Frequency, Daytime = Lower Frequency.
explanation: Rules of thumb: shorter distance means lower frequency; daytime means higher frequency (night means lower).
background: HF band selection rules of thumb: farther = higher frequency; daytime = higher frequency, night = lower. 2 MHz (MF) for up to ~150-300 NM; 4-6 MHz for short to medium range and at night; 8 MHz is the all-round band; 12-16 MHz for long range by day; 22 MHz for very long range in daylight. Starting from what worked last time at the same hour usually works.

question: A ship has been communicating effectively on 16 MHz during daylight hours with a shore station at a distance of 3200 miles. Toward late afternoon and evening what effect would be noticed?
choices: Communications should gradually deteriorate and become impossible on this frequency at night.
Communications should be maintained with slight improvement in the signal received from the shore station.
The gray line effect will prevent communications after dark.
Communications should improve and peak at night.
explanation: 16 MHz long-distance paths need the daytime ionosphere. As darkness falls, the MUF drops below 16 MHz and the signal fades out.
background: Why the rules work: the D layer (daytime only) absorbs low frequencies, so 2-4 MHz signals are weak by day and improve at night; the F layer's MUF (Maximum Usable Frequency) is high by day and drops at night, so 16-22 MHz paths open in daylight and close after dark. Short distances on high bands fall into the skip zone. Coast station free signals show which band is open.

question: A ship at anchor has been communicating with a shore station approximately 350 miles distant on a frequency in the 4 MHz band through early afternoon. Toward the late afternoon and evening, what effect should be noticed?

question: The Distress Alarm sounds and the screen readout no longer contains the particulars of the Distress:

background: Automatic DSC switching: when a DSC call proposes a follow-on channel, the transceiver may switch automatically. question: A DSC Distress alert is received by your vessel and your transceiver frequency display reads: Transmit = 4207.5 kHz and Receive = 4207.5 kHz with J3E emission -- what information can you infer from this?
choices: The DSC call requested voice on 4207.5 kHz simplex but the requested alternate frequency is improper.

The DSC controller decoded the requested voice frequency as 4207.5 kHz simplex and your DSC controller has automatically set-up your transceiver and therefore the requested alternate frequency is correct.
The DSC call came in on 4 MHz DSC. You should set-up your transmitter and respond on the appropriate voice follow-on frequency of 4177.5 kHz.
